messages.subject: Alternatives or Workarounds for googleVis Dynamic Map
messages.subject_clean: Alternatives or Workarounds for googleVis Dynamic Map
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

I have been using googleVis to make interactive, dynamic maps as described by Ryan Peek here <http://www.noamross.net/blog/2015/2/20/mapping-in-R-peek-tobias.html>. The described method makes a very nice, clean map with markers that will display additional information about a point when clicked on. Since this outputs as html/javascript, it would be great to host on our project website. Unfortunately, Google Charts API (which the googleVis package utilizes) only allows for a map of 400 markers at a time (as described in the documentation here <https://developers.google.com/chart/interactive/docs/gallery/geomap>. Some of the datasets I would like to map have over 3000 records! Does anyone know of a similar alternative for making a dynamic, web-hostable map, or possibly a way to trick Google Charts into displaying more records? I don't have much hope for the latter solution, but I figured this was the place to ask.

Cheers,
Nate Hamlet

messages.body_plain:
Hi nate,

The leaflet package (whose predecessor, leafletR, was presented by Michele in that same video), doesn't have any limits to markers as far as I know, and is very good for making web-embeddable, dynamic maps: https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/

You will likely want to use clustering so that thousands of markers don't appear at once - this is a big computational load for any browser.  Clustering groups nearby markers together until the zoom is high enough to distinguish them.  This keeps too many points from ever having to be rendered at once.  Details at https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/markers.html#marker-clusters

This is a bit of an ugly solution, but it seems to work:

# import and fix Erica's data:

datasample <- read.csv("~/Desktop/brdug/drug-datasample.csv", header=FALSE, comment.char="#")

# I think we first need to split this into one data frame per region:

header = which(datasample[,1]=="1. Codigo producto")
region1 = datasample[header[1]:(header[2]-4),]
region2 = datasample[header[2]:(header[3]-4),]
region3 = datasample[header[3]:nrow(datasample),]

# Now change the names of the variables
names(region1) = c("Condigo", "R1_Casos", "R1_%", "R1_Acumulado")
names(region2) = c("Condigo", "R2_Casos", "R2_%", "R2_Acumulado")
names(region3) = c("Condigo", "R3_Casos", "R3_%", "R3_Acumulado")

# get rid of the first lines
region1 = region1[-1,]
region2 = region3[-1,]
region3 = region3[-1,]

# Now merge the data sets together

fulldata = merge(region1, region2, by = "Condigo", all.x = T, all.y = T)
fulldata = merge(fulldata, region3, by = "Condigo", all.x = T, all.y = T)

# However, for a lot of analyses, you might want your data in this format instead:
region1$region = rep(1, nrow(region1))
region2$region = rep(2, nrow(region2))
region3$region = rep(3, nrow(region3))

names(region1) = c("Condigo", "Casos", "Percent", "Acumulado", "region")
names(region2) = c("Condigo", "Casos", "Percent", "Acumulado", "region")

I took a bit of a different approach, but it seems to work.

## Data
pp <- "~/Downloads/drug-datasample.csv"

## Read in data as lines to find where to separate
doc <- readLines(pp)

## Look for headings
idx <- grep("AREA", doc)

## Length of each table, accounting for spaces before and after "AREA" line
nr <- diff(c(idx, length(doc) + 2)) - 2

## Read in each table separately
ans <- lapply(seq_along(idx), function(i)
    read.csv(pp, skip = idx[i] + 1, nrows = nr[i] - 2))

## Get area info
area_info <- strsplit(doc[idx], ",")

## Add area info to data.frames
ans <- lapply(seq_along(ans), function(i) {
    x <- ans[[i]]
    x$area <- area_info[[i]][1]
    x$area_nm <- area_info[[i]][2]
    return(x)
    })

## Combine
do.call(rbind, ans)

Matt

Hi,

Calvin is correct - the issue is that the function only takes a single lat/long pair at a time. You can solve this by looping over your lat/long pairs.

One thing you need to check is your allowed calls to the API per day and per min/hour. Many APIs limit how many and how quickly you can query them. Depending on your network latency, you might exceed the limits and get your API key/IP blocked. Check the terms of the API so you don't potentially block the campus IP from the API. You can slow down your requests if needed by using Sys.sleep().

Lastly, scanning over the source code, the walkscoreAPI package has a pretty poor implementation and WILL break in some situations. You should wrap your call to the API with try() to avoid this from breaking your whole loop.

If the problems with the walkscoreAPI package are cropping up a lot, it would be simple to write your own function to query the API that would be much more robust.

Matt

Sure - Duncan could probably do much better than I, but here is a stab at it.

You can look at the function call if you type in its name without the parentheses. Walking through the function:

getWS
function (x, y, key)
{
    URL <- paste("http://api.walkscore.com/score?lat=", y, "&lon=",
        x, "&wsapikey=", key, sep = "")
    X <- character(0)
    X <- c(X, scan(file = URL, what = "", sep = "\n", quiet = TRUE))
...

At the head of the function, they do not have any checks in place to make sure the input is in the correct format and they use scan(), which does not ensure a valid request is constructed. Better would be to use a function like getForm().

Next,

...
    string <- X[grep("<walkscore>", X)]
    string2 <- X[grep("<description>", X)]
    string3 <- X[grep("<updated>", X)]
...

The API returns XML by default. They are parsing this themselves, rather than use existing functions that know how to read XML.

Next (and probably the worst),

 if (status == 1) {
        walk <- strsplit(string, "<walkscore>")
        walk2 <- gsub("</walkscore>", "", walk[[1]][2])
        wscore <- as.numeric(walk2)
        ...
   }
    else {
        wscore <- "NA"
        descr <- "NA"
        ...
    }

The API returns a lot of information about why a request did not return results via the status codes, but all this information is thrown out and NAs are returned. There is nothing more maddening than making a call to an API and getting unexpected results with no explanation. It would be best to preserve this information so the user can diagnose errors.

An example of how it could be done better would be something like this (Note: I requested JSON rather than XML so I can use the fromJSON function. Warning: I am just throwing this together and have not tested it.)

require(RCurl)
require(jsonlite)

getWS <- function(x, y, key)
{
    if(!(is.numeric(x) & is.numeric(y)))
        stop("Lat/Long must be in decimal degrees.")

    doc <- getForm("http://api.walkscore.com/score?",
                   format = "json", lat = y, lon = x,
                   wsapikey = key)

    fromJSON(doc)
}

If you wanted to get really fancy, you could have the function return the meaning of the error codes as well, as found at the bottom of https://www.walkscore.com/professional/api.php.

Let me know if you have any questions,

Matt

messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: Constraints vs. Bounds in the R Optimization Infrastructure (ROI) library
messages.body_plain:
I tend to use the nloptr package for optimization problems rather than ROI, but the concepts are the same.  Bounds are absolute limits on the range of values, while constraints are limits on *relationships* between values.  For instance, if I am minimizing Z, which is a function of X and Y, bounds could be -10 < X < 10, or 3 < Y < 6.  Constraints can be more complex. I could impose an *inequality* constraint of Y < 10 - X, which would tell the solver to find the lowest value of Z that falls below that diagonal line on the X-Y plane.  An *equality* constraint, Y = 10 - X, would try to find the point ON that line with the lowest value of Z.

In theory, bounds are just simple versions of constraints, but they're usually handled separately by the solvers called by optim(), ROI, nloptr, optimx, etc, and thus are entered as separate arguments into the optimization function.  Different solvers can typically handle different levels of complexity in constraints, such as only linear constraints (like the example above), or quadratic constraints.

- Noam

Hi Bic,

You can do this with the sapply() or vapply() functions, which will perform a function you specify on each element in your matrix. My approach was to use the y matrix create another matrix of TRUE’s and FALSE’s corresponding to the bad and good elements of x. Then I set all of the elements of x that are in the same position as the TRUE’s to NA.

Let me know if this doesn’t get you what you want!

Mike

x<-matrix(c(1,5,6,3,2,1), nrow=2, ncol=3)
y<-matrix(c(132,15,36,103,2000,154), nrow=2, ncol=3)

# This function will take an integer, decompose it into a 32 element vector of "raw" values, take the 3rd element (corresponding to the 4's place) and then converts that value to TRUE or FALSE.
badCellCheck <- function(x) {
  as.logical(intToBits(x)[3])
}

# We can use sapply or vapply to perform a function to every element in an object (a matrix in this case). We apply our badCellCheck() function to each element of y, and then use the structure() function to specify that we want the result to have the same dimensions as y.
badCellIdx <- structure(sapply(y, FUN= badCellCheck), dim= dim(y))

# Here is an alternative way to do the same thing as above. vapply() will be a bit faster because we also specify that the result of the function is a logical (a TRUE or a FALSE). Since R doesn't have to figure this out on its own, this will perform faster which could matter if your matrix is really large.
badCellIdx <- structure(vapply(y, FUN= badCellCheck, FUN.VALUE= logical(1)), dim= dim(y))

# Here is the result of that operation:
badCellIdx

# Now we can use the matrix of TRUE's and FALSE's as an indexing matrix. All of the elements in the x matrix that correspond to the TRUE elements in the badCellIdx matrix will be assigned NA.
x[badCellIdx] <- NA
x

Hi D-RUG,

I'm working with several frequency distributions that I want to compare. They are size distributions of particles suspended in water before and after being exposed to filter feeding animals. What I want to do is ask whether these distributions change over time relative to a control without filter feeders. Essentially, is filter feeding by the animals I sampled size selective?

Here's a visual example:

Let's say the first panel shows the kernel density estimate of the particle size distribution from a filter feeder-free control before (green) and after (red) an experimental trial and the second panel shows the same for a treatment with a filter feeder. The x axis is cut off but goes from small to large particle sizes (the sizes are estimated using flow cytometry).

I have many of these distributions from different treatments and trials, so showing a couple dozen kernel density plots is visually overwhelming. Also, the differences between the distributions tends to be small, to my eye anyway, so there is a lot of overlap in the different panels (facets here for ggplot).

Can anyone suggest how I might better visualize the changes in size frequency relative to controls? I have tried binning data into size classes and finding the differences in each bin for each treatment, but I'm not totally satisfied with that approach. I'm also interested in a statistical test of these differences in distributions (again, relative to controls for each trial).

I would really appreciate any suggestions of strategies I might take to better visualize these data and to conduct a sensible statistical test. I've done some t-tests and mixed effects models already.

Thank you very much,

Matt

messages.body_plain:
1) Given the shape of the distributions (long-tailed), it may make sense to visualize density of the log values.
2) You could reduce one of these plots to a single value by calculating Kullback-Leibler divergence between the distributions, which measures how much of the information in one distribution is captured by the other. (Note that it is not transitive, i.e., KLD(A, B) != KLD(B, A) ),  Its implemented in several R packages.  I have no insight as to which is best, but the math is relatively simple so any of them is probably fine.  Then you can compare these values visually across your treatments.  The Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic is another such metric, and has an associated nonparametric test.
3) Maybe a GLM on the log values, or a Gamma GLM would be appropriate?

Hello all,

If I am making a graph using ggplot, I can plot a trendline using geom_smooth()

For example:

df = data.frame(x=c(1,2,3,4,5,6,7), y= c(2,4,3,5,8,9,10))

p = ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm")

Is there a way of extracting the information on the linear model used to plot the line and standard errors? Coefficients and R2 and such? I can always just use the lm function, but it would seem to save a step if I could make ggplot report it for me.

An alternative strategy is to use the 'augment' method from package 'broom' to add columns to teh original data based on the lm fit. Then, you could run ggplot on that data and model fit data without geom_smooth.

But, if you'd rather try to get the model out of ggplot objects, the results from some poking around I just did may be helpful.

str(p$layers[[2]]$stat_params) # the 2 here will need to correspond with the geom_smooth layer...
List of 4
 $ na.rm  : logi FALSE
 $ method : chr "lm"
 $ formula:Class 'formula'  language y ~ x
  .. ..- attr(*, ".Environment")=<environment: 0x36e9110>
 $ se     : logi TRUE

You could maybe write a small function to run this fit on the data in the plot object. LIkely there's something in ggplot2 that would be useful for this, possibly the predictdf function: https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/59c503b8e1cacf1f9264d1e233b7a305916905d6/R/stat-smooth-methods.r

Hope this helps,
